paras: The reported intimidation of Black residents at Shelbyville, Indiana, was one of several "attempts at intimidation" named in a Cincinnati dispatch of August 12, 1880, during the presidential campaign. The dispatch gave no details of what happened there, and it is the only report of the episode found.

The dispatch, printed under the heading "Intimidation in Indiana," opened by charging that "Demeratic threats of driving the negroes out of Indiana" were being carried out "in at least three counties." Its main example was an attack the previous morning near Columbus, Indiana, where a masked band it called "Kuklux" broke into the house of a Black man, Joshua Mack, threatened to hang him, and let him go on condition that he leave at once. According to the dispatch, the attackers said they meant to drive all Black people out of the county before the election, and they later stoned the house of the white farmer who rented Mack his land.

Shelbyville appears only in the dispatch's last sentence: "At Bluffton and Shelbyville similar attempts at intimidation have been made." The dispatch named no victims or perpetrators there, described no specific acts, and did not say when the attempts took place beyond placing them before August 12.

The account located ran in the Somerset Herald of Somerset, Pennsylvania, on August 25, nearly two weeks after the Cincinnati dateline. Its framing was partisan and hostile to the attackers: it called Mack "inoffensive," described the band's "vile oaths," and laid the campaign to the Democrats, while Shelbyville received a single line. No Indiana report, no detailed wire story and no Black-press account of events at Shelbyville appears in the coverage, which leaves the episode resting on that one sentence.
